newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul gov't says new steel mill "not desirable".
newsitem.headline: Seoul gov't says new steel mill "not desirable".

text.p: South Korea's trade ministry said on Thursday that the construction of a new integrated steel mill was "not desirable" for the country.

Leem Lae-gue, director-general of the ministry's basic industry bureau, told reporters the ministry reached the opinion after a comprehensive overview of the expected impact of such a mill on existing businesses and market trends.

Leem did not directly name Hyundai Group, but his remarks are widely seen as being pointed towards the giant conglomerate, which has said it planned to build a mill to meet demand from its affiliates, industry sources said.
A spokesman for Hyundai, South Korea's largest conglomerate in terms of assets, declined to comment on the announcement.
Rumours have circulated that the government was opposed to Hyundai's plan, but Leem's were the first official remarks on the government stand concerning new steel mills.
Seoul has given up controls on most private business activities, but maintains restrictions on certain industries requiring foreign technology.
The steel sector has no such barriers against new entries but analysts say it would be almost impossible for Hyundai to go ahead with the plan without the government's support.
The ministry plans to submit its position to the Industrial Development Council meeting on Friday.

The council, an advisory body made up of senior government officials, professors, researchers and journalists, also plans to discuss the government's campaign to improve the national economy's competitiveness, a ministry spokesman said.
In July, Hyundai said its unit, Inchon Iron and Steel Co, would build a new steel mill capable of producing six million tonnes a year by 2004.
Hyundai has revealed no details of its investment plan, but analysts estimate the project would cost the conglomerate a minimum of 10 trillion won.
